# We have NA for ECSIdealAgeEntryBaseline, TrustCreche, BreastFeedLength, NormsOpposedN, AffordCostBaseline, NumberChildren we may want to impute them

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Our recipe. Our task is a classification task because our taget is a categorical variable. 
# step_unkown turns NAs into "unknown" becuse tidymodels and our algo do not like NAs

rf_recipe <- recipe(target ~ ., data = train_df)  %>%
  step_unknown(Primipare,FmlyIncomeBaseline,
                 IncomeBaseline, 
               TrustCreche, 
               DeprivHolidays,
               BreastFeedIntend,
               InformalReciprocity, 
             TrustAssMat,
             TrustFam,
             TrustFriend,
             CoupleCohabiting,
             AccessEasy5) %>% 
  # We dummify everything
  step_dummy(Educ3, 
             Educ3Dad,
             DiscountRate,
                          AffordSubsidiesBaseline,
             AffordNMCostWBBaseline,
             AffordOppCostBaseline,
             AffordNMCostCareerBaseline,
             DiscountRate,
             AccessHoursBaseline, 
             BirthPlace3, 
             FmlyIncomeBaseline,
                 IncomeBaseline, 
             TrustCreche, 
             LikertReturnHKBaseline, 
             DeprivHolidays) %>% 
  step_impute_knn(NormsOpposedN,  # we impute missing values for the numerical variables using knn
                  AffordCostBaseline,
                  BreastFeedLength,
                  NumberChildren,
                  neighbors = 5) %>% 
  step_YeoJohnson(NormsOpposedN, AffordCostBaseline, BreastFeedLength,NumberChildren) # some variables are skewed. We transform them using YeoJohson that can also deal with missing values

## RUN THE RANDOM FOREST

# In the REAL DEFINITIVE VERSION you should also tune the number of trees, or at least generate 150 of them.
rf_spec <- rand_forest(mtry = tune(), # 100 is a low side. Do at least 150 
                       trees = 10, # if I tune it, it takes forever to run
                       min_n = tune()) %>%
  set_mode("classification") %>% # IMPORTANT! It can also deal with classes and influence the loss function
  set_engine("partykit")


# Flooow: specify what transformations (recipe) will be done and what algo will be fitted in a first step
initial_flow <- workflow() %>% # create the initial workflow
  add_recipe(rf_recipe) %>%
  add_model(rf_spec)


# The argument finalize is key because tidymodels needs to look
# at the data to figure out how many features there are.

# We need to tell tidymodels which parameters need to be tuned. It can conveniently be done with this chunk of code

# In this version we are not tuning the number of trees, but we could.
# We tune mtry and min_n the number of obs in each terminal leaves (you don't want one leaf == 1 obs that's overfitting)
# mtry is the number of features that are randomly selected at each split. It is a good idea to tune it because it can have a big impact on the performance of the model
# Doing this is an argument if I have a lot of predictors/features. At each round, it is only a subsample of predictors that is used. 
rf_para <- extract_parameter_set_dials(rf_spec) %>% # extract the tuning parameters
  finalize(train_df) # here we have only 2 because we set trees to 100 not tune()
# finalize(train): we need to know the maximum number of features we could fit because it has not looked at the data yet
# it tells tidymodel that he can look at the data quickly to see how many features there are in the data

set.seed(20) # for reproducibility

# Set the tuning grid
# The tuning grid is the set of values of the tuning parameters we seek to evaluate. The larger the better
rf_grid <- grid_latin_hypercube(rf_para,  # we use a latin hypercube here. 
                                size = 50, # 25 random combinations of mtry and min_n LOW! Increase in real life. There are good chances that the "true" combination is not in there
                                variogram_range = 0.75, # explore the space of the hyperparameters
                                original = TRUE)
set.seed(30)

# Set the cross validation. 
# Ideally, we would need to do repetitions of the cross validation to increase the robustness of the results. 
# Do this in the final version with the repeats = 10 argument
# it will create 9 training folds and 1 validation fold. It will do this 10 times.
cv_folds <- vfold_cv(train_df, v = 10, strata = target) # stratified CV

# Set the metrics used: accuracy or cohen's kappa or F1 for a classification task (or AUC)
rf_metrics <- metric_set(accuracy) # classification task

doParallel::registerDoParallel() # used parallel cores to run the computation

# tune the model, with the cross validation method defined, the grid and the metrics you set
rf_tune <- initial_flow %>%
  tune_grid(cv_folds, grid = rf_grid, metrics = rf_metrics)


# select the best parameters for the model the tuning found
rf_best <- select_best(rf_tune)
rf_best# Trees again with X features at each time and X obs at terminal leaves
# 34 features, and 19 obs in terminal leaves

# Update the model with the best parameters found
rf_updated <- finalize_model(rf_spec,
                             rf_best) 

# add this to the initial workflow
workflow_new <- initial_flow %>%
  update_model(rf_updated)

# Fit the model on the training set
rf_fit_final <- workflow_new %>%
  fit(data = train_df) # fit on the training set

# Fit the model on the test set to evaluate performance
# Performance on the test set
rf_fit_final %>%
  predict(test_df) %>%
  bind_cols(test_df) %>%
  metrics(truth = target, estimate = .pred_class)
# the accuracy is great but the kappa not that much (average)
# see if tuning the trees improve this in the future


```

## Node importance

```{r}

# NODE IMPORTANCE
# You need to give up on partykit to get some info on variable importance, so we have to do it again

mod_rf <-rand_forest() %>%
  set_engine("ranger",
             num.threads = parallel::detectCores(), # to do it in parallel 
             importance = "permutation", # different way of assessing importance: to avoid that one variable always arrives after another one
             verbose = TRUE) %>% # keeps a lot of details for us
  set_mode("classification") %>%
  set_args(trees = 50)#update here

# Same steps again to fit the model
# workflow

# Reminder: even the prof could not explain this code 
rf_flow <- workflow() %>% 
  add_model(mod_rf) %>% 
  add_recipe(rf_recipe)

# With new code for using future
library(future)
set.seed(100)
plan(multisession)

fit_rf <- fit_resamples(
  rf_flow,
  cv_folds,
  metrics = metric_set(accuracy),
  control = control_resamples(verbose = TRUE,
                              save_pred = TRUE,
                              extract = function(x) x) # the function return the value of the prediction
)

library(forcats)
library(tidyverse)
# extract roots
# code to extract the images
rf_tree_roots <- function(x){
  map_chr(1:50, # 50 trees
          ~ranger::treeInfo(x, tree = .)[1, "splitvarName"]) # extract how we made the splits
}

rf_roots <- function(x){
  x %>% 
    select(.extracts) %>% 
    unnest(cols = c(.extracts)) %>% 
    mutate(fit = map(.extracts,
                     ~.x$fit$fit$fit), # dig deep to find 
           oob_rmse = map_dbl(fit,
                              ~sqrt(.x$prediction.error)), # out of bag error: some items are left out of the training set during CV and we can see how well the model does on them 
           roots = map(fit, 
                       ~rf_tree_roots(.)) 
    ) %>% 
    select(roots) %>% 
    unnest(cols = c(roots))
}

roots_data <- rf_roots(fit_rf)

# Group the data by roots and count the occurrences of each root
root_counts <- roots_data %>% 
  group_by(roots) %>% 
  count()

# Filter out roots with counts greater than 75
filtered_root_counts <- root_counts %>% 
  filter(n > 45) # you can modify it. The prof set 75 but with 75 on this one it removed everything. The number seems quite arbitrary

# Arrange the data in descending order of counts
sorted_root_counts <- filtered_root_counts %>% 
  arrange(desc(n))

# Create a bar plot
plot <- ggplot(sorted_root_counts, aes(x = fct_reorder(roots, n), y = n)) +
  geom_col() + 
  coord_flip() + 
  labs(x = "Root", y = "Count")

# Display the plot
print(plot)
```

# interpr

```{r}
## Contribution

library(DALEXtra) # if not called already
# DALEX want to know a couple of things in the explainer
explainer <- explain_tidymodels( # create the  explainer
  model = rf_fit_final, # what is the model
  data = test_df, # what do you want to explain? The test data? The train data? Something else?
  y = test_df$target # what is the target variable?
)


# With that, you can calculate a pdp plot

pdp <- model_profile( # create the plot
  explainer,
  variables = "NormsOpposedN", # in theory you could put two predictors
  N = NULL
)

as_tibble(pdp$agr_profiles) %>% # rely on agr profiles_attribute
  ggplot(aes(`_x_`, `_yhat_`)) + # yhat is the predicted values after the averaging process of the pdp 
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_rug(sides = "b") + # add a rug: what are the actual values in the test set? Get a sense of whether we could be extrapolating a bit too much
  labs(
    x = "Number of ppl around you that you think they think EC is bad",
    y = "Predicted probabilty of wanting to use daycare",
    color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_bw()


# BREAKDOWN PLOT

# We select (for instance) the 1st test sample
temp1 <- test_df[7,!(names(test_df) %in% "target")] # we remove the target variable through the -1
temp1


# Create the breakdown plot using the explainer
bd1 <- predict_parts(explainer = explainer,
                     new_observation = temp1)


# plot
plot(bd1) 
# we are adding to the predicted probabibily that country X is a democracy
# the scale is a probability scale


# SHAPLY VALUES
library(forcats)

set.seed(1995)
shap <- predict_parts(explainer = explainer,
                      new_observation = test_df[, !(names(test_df) %in% "target")], # remove the target
                      type = "shap", 
                      B = 20)

average_shapley <- shap %>% 
  group_by(variable) %>% 
  summarise(contribution = mean(contribution)) %>% 
  arrange(desc(abs(contribution)))


shap %>%
  group_by(variable) %>%
  mutate(mean_val = mean(contribution)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(variable = fct_reorder(variable, abs(mean_val))) %>% # reorder the variables according to their contribution in term of their absolute value
  ggplot(aes(contribution, variable, fill = mean_val > 0)) +
  geom_col(data = ~distinct(., variable, mean_val), 
           aes(mean_val, variable), 
           alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5) +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(y = NULL) +
  theme_bw()

```

  ggplot(aes(`_x_`, `_yhat_`)) + # yhat is the predicted values after the averaging process of the pdp 
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_rug(sides = "b") + # add a rug: what are the actual values in the test set? Get a sense of whether we could be extrapolating a bit too much
  labs(
    x = "Trust in daycare",
    y = "Predicted probabilty of a democracy",
    color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_bw()


# BREAKDOWN PLOT

# We select (for instance) the 1st test sample
temp1 <- test_df[1, !(names(test_df) %in% "target")]# we remove the target variable 
temp1


# Create the breakdown plot using the explainer
bd1 <- predict_parts(explainer = explainer,
                     new_observation = temp1)

# plot
plot(bd1) 
# we are adding to the predicted probabibily that country X is a democracy
# the scale is a probability scale


# SHAPLY VALUES
library(forcats)

set.seed(1995)
shap <- predict_parts(explainer = explainer,
                      new_observation = test_df[, !(names(test_df) %in% "target")], # remove the target
                      type = "shap", 
                      B = 100)

average_shapley <- shap %>% 
  group_by(variable) %>% 
  summarise(contribution = mean(contribution)) %>% 
  arrange(desc(abs(contribution)))


shap %>%
  group_by(variable) %>%
  mutate(mean_val = mean(contribution)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(variable = fct_reorder(variable, abs(mean_val))) %>% # reorder the variables according to their contribution in term of their absolute value
  ggplot(aes(contribution, variable, fill = mean_val > 0)) +
  geom_col(data = ~distinct(., variable, mean_val), 
           aes(mean_val, variable), 
           alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5) +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(y = NULL) +
  theme_bw()

  step_unknown(ECSIdealAgeEntryBaseline,

         #    AccessEasyBaseline,

rf_spec <- rand_forest(mtry = tune(), # 100 is a low side. Do at least 150 
                       trees = 50, # Each of 90% of data we set aside in the 10 fold CV, we are going to fit 100 trees
                       min_n = tune()) %>%
  set_mode("classification") %>% # IMPORTANT! It can also deal with classes and influence the loss function
  set_engine("partykit")


# Flooow
initial_flow <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(rf_recipe) %>%
  add_model(rf_spec)

# We are going to use 10-fold CV AND bootsrap
# We fit trees on each fold, then bootstrap, create another fold to add another layer of validation


# The argument finalize is key because tidymodels needs to look
# at the data to figure out how many features there are.
rf_para <- extract_parameter_set_dials(rf_spec) %>% # extract the tuning parameters
  finalize(train_df) # here we have only 2 because we set trees to 100 not tune()
# finalize(train): we need to know the maximum number of features we could fit because it has not looked at the data yet
# it tells tidymodel that he can look at the data quickly to see how many features there are in the data

set.seed(20)
rf_grid <- grid_latin_hypercube(rf_para, 
                                size = 25, # 25 random combinations of mtry and min_n LOW! Increase in real life. There are good chances that the "true" combination is not in there
                                variogram_range = 0.75,
                                original = TRUE)
set.seed(30)
cv_folds <- vfold_cv(train_df, v = 10)
rf_metrics <- metric_set(accuracy)

doParallel::registerDoParallel()
rf_tune <- initial_flow %>%
  tune_grid(cv_folds, grid = rf_grid, metrics = rf_metrics)
rf_best <- select_best(rf_tune)
rf_best


rf_updated <- finalize_model(rf_spec,
                             rf_best) # Trees again avec 5 features at each time and 18 obs at termina nodes

workflow_new <- initial_flow %>%
  update_model(rf_updated)

rf_fit_final <- workflow_new %>%
  fit(data = train_df) # fit on the training set


# Performance on the test set
rf_fit_final %>%
  predict(test_df) %>%
  bind_cols(test_df) %>%
  metrics(truth = target, estimate = .pred_class)

## Node importance

```{r}

# NODE IMPORTANCE
# You need to give up on partykit to get some info on variable importance, so we have to do it again

mod_rf <-rand_forest() %>%
  set_engine("ranger",
             num.threads = parallel::detectCores(), # to do it in parallel 
             importance = "permutation", # different way of assessing importance: to avoid that one variable always arrives after another one
             verbose = TRUE) %>% # keeps a lot of details for us
  set_mode("classification") %>%
  set_args(trees = 50)


rf_flow <- workflow() %>% 
  add_model(mod_rf) %>% 
  add_recipe(rf_recipe)

# With new code for using future
library(future)
set.seed(100)
plan(multisession)

fit_rf <- fit_resamples(
  rf_flow,
  cv_folds,
  metrics = metric_set(accuracy),
  control = control_resamples(verbose = TRUE,
                              save_pred = TRUE,
                              extract = function(x) x) # the function return the value of the prediction
)

library(forcats)
library(tidyverse)
# extract roots
# code to extract the images
rf_tree_roots <- function(x){
  map_chr(1:50, # 50 trees
          ~ranger::treeInfo(x, tree = .)[1, "splitvarName"]) # extract how we made the splits
}

rf_roots <- function(x){
  x %>% 
    select(.extracts) %>% 
    unnest(cols = c(.extracts)) %>% 
    mutate(fit = map(.extracts,
                     ~.x$fit$fit$fit), # dig deep to find 
           oob_rmse = map_dbl(fit,
                              ~sqrt(.x$prediction.error)), # oob error
           roots = map(fit, 
                       ~rf_tree_roots(.)) 
    ) %>% 
    select(roots) %>% 
    unnest(cols = c(roots))
}

roots_data <- rf_roots(fit_rf)

# Group the data by roots and count the occurrences of each root
root_counts <- roots_data %>% 
  group_by(roots) %>% 
  count()

# Filter out roots with counts greater than 75
filtered_root_counts <- root_counts %>% 
  filter(n > 75)

# Arrange the data in descending order of counts
sorted_root_counts <- filtered_root_counts %>% 
  arrange(desc(n))

# Create a bar plot
plot <- ggplot(sorted_root_counts, aes(x = fct_reorder(roots, n), y = n)) +
  geom_col() + 
  coord_flip() + 
  labs(x = "Root", y = "Count")

# Display the plot
print(plot)
```
